newsitem.title: INDIA: No fast confidence return seen in India new issues.
newsitem.headline: No fast confidence return seen in India new issues.

text.p: India's battered new issues market is unlikely to revive in the near-term as investor apathy and depressed stock markets take their toll, analysts said on Thursday.

"The primary market has suffered severe loss of confidence," said Amit Dalal at broking firm Amit Nalinkant Share and Stock Brokers. "People have lost heavily ... every issue in recent months is quoting below its premium levels."
Fresh issues, both equity and debt, by companies in August shrunk to 3.63 billion rupees against 16.75 billion in July, says Prime Database which tracks the primary market.

"Subscription by genuine retail investors has been totally absent and is not likely to improve at least till the next 3-4 months," said Nitin Gandhi, vice-president at Prabhudas Lilladhar, a brokerage firm.
"There have been many false promises by issuers who have just not been able to deliver," he said.
And the market is still beset by the problem of new issuers, deliberately pitching their issue at too high a premium, analysts said.
"Unscrupulous promoters who issued shares at high premiums and vanished after listing continue to affect investor sentiment," said an analyst at a top underwriting firm.
The number of companies that entered the market in August fell to 87 from 99 in the previous month.

Concerns over political stability -- after the formation of a loosely bound 13-party coalition last June--, a liquidity crunch and a disappointing 1996/97 budget have dragged shares down in the last two months, analysts said.
The benchmark 30-share index of the Bombay Stock Exchange has lost 550 points or nearly 14 percent from the year's peak of 4,069 on June 18.
The index ended at 3,516.90 on Wednesday.
Foreign funds were the major buyers in Indian bourses in the first half of calendar 1996, but this demand is now slowing.

Net foreign portfolio investment on Indian bourses fell sharply to $66.7 million in the first 29 days of August from $302.4 million in July 1996, figures released by the market regulator Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) show.
Prime Database said the absence of debt issues which flooded the market in July also added to the drastic fall in cash raised by companies.
"Debt issues which dominated the market in the previous few months were absent in August."
In the past few months, bond floats have mopped up 55 billion rupees.
With equity-shy investors lured to the debt market, new bond offers are expected to garner another 50-60 billion rupees in the next few months.

In August two mutual funds -- floated by Templeton Asset Management Company and ITC Threadneedle Asset Management Company -- were compelled to extend their closing date by nearly a week to achieve their target of 500 million rupees each.
"The issue of good stocks to investors at discounts could help in reviving interest of retail investors," Prabhudas' Gandhi said.
